About: The Parallel-Axis Theorem

Source

Topic
Rigid-body rotation — moment of inertia
Concept
The extra inertia from moving the axis away from the centre of mass is m·s² — the same for every shape.
Serves
JEE / NCERT Class 11 rotational mechanics.
Misconception
That the shift term depends on the shape of the body. It does not — Icm does; the shift is m·s² for everything.

Guided Inquiry

The axis at the centre

Right now the rotation axis (the ★) sits AT the centre of mass. The shift bar — the orange contribution m·s² — reads exactly zero. The only inertia is Icm, which depends on the shape and mass.

Now imagine dragging the axis outward, all the way to s = 0.5 m. With the default mass m = 2 kg, the shift term will become 0.5 kg·m². What do you predict it becomes at HALF that offset, s = 0.25 m?

Predict: double the offset

Start at s = 0.25 m. If you then double the offset to s = 0.5 m, what does the shift term m·s² do?

Now drag the ★ and verify

Drag the ★ from s = 0.25 m out to s = 0.5 m, keeping the default m = 2 kg. Watch the orange bar (m·s²). At s = 0.25 m it reads 0.125 kg·m². At s = 0.5 m it reads 0.5 kg·m² — exactly four times as much.

Notice that the teal bar (Icm) does not move: the shape is not being deformed, only the axis is being relocated.

Predict: change the shape

Keep the offset at, say, s = 0.25 m. Switch the shape from disc to hoop. Both have the same mass and radius. What happens to the orange shift bar (m·s²)?

The theorem, in one sentence

The moment of inertia about any axis parallel to the one through the centre of mass is I = Icm + m·s². The teal bar is the shape-dependent Icm; the orange bar is the shape-INDEPENDENT shift.

Because m·s² is never negative, the centre of mass is the cheapest axis there is — every other parallel axis costs strictly more. Free play from here: try any shape, mass and offset.

The Physics

Parallel-Axis Theorem — What Moving the Axis Costs · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A flat body can spin about different axes that all point the same way. Here one axis passes through its centre of mass and a second, the ★, can be dragged away from it. The sim shows what that move does to the moment of inertia.

What you'll learn

  • How the moment of inertia changes when the rotation axis is moved away from the centre of mass.
  • What part of that change depends on the shape and what part does not.
  • Why the centre of mass is a special place for the axis.
The body, its two axes, and the two stacked bars. The bar heights here are only a sketch.

What's on screen

  • Body (teal): a disc, hoop, sphere or rod of radius or length 0.50 m, swinging about the ★. A dashed crosshair rides on its centre of mass.
  • ★ offset axis (orange): the fixed axis the body turns about. Drag it sideways. A grey line marks s, the distance to the centre of mass.
  • Dashed circle (orange): the path the centre of mass follows around the ★.
  • Two stacked bars on the right: a teal bar Icm with an orange bar m·s² on top, and the total I above them.
See itStart with the axis at the centre of mass. Watch for: the ★ sitting on the body's centre, a teal bar reading 0.250, and no orange bar.

03

About the centre of mass, I = c m R² by shape

With the axis through the centre of mass the moment of inertia is Icm = c·m·R². The number c comes from the shape, so it fixes the teal bar:

  • Mass packed near the middle gives a small c.
  • Mass out at the rim gives a large c, so a hoop beats a disc of the same mass and radius.

Here R = 0.50 m. For the rod, R is its full length. Doubling m doubles Icm.

ShapecIcm at m = 2.0 kg
Disc1/20.250 kg·m²
Hoop10.500 kg·m²
Solid sphere2/50.200 kg·m²
Rod, about its centre1/120.042 kg·m²
See itSwitch to the hoop with the axis at the centre. Watch for: the teal bar doubling from 0.250 to 0.500, with still no orange bar.
04

Moving the axis by s adds m s² to I

For any axis parallel to the one through the centre of mass, at distance s from it, the parallel-axis theorem gives:

I = Icm + m s²
The orange bar is the shift m·s², stacked on the teal Icm.

The shift is quadratic in s, so doubling s multiplies it by 4. It is linear in m, so doubling m doubles it. For a 2.0 kg disc:

sm·s²I
000.250 kg·m²
0.25 m0.125 kg·m²0.375 kg·m²
0.50 m0.500 kg·m²0.750 kg·m²

The teal bar does not move. The body is not deformed, only the axis is relocated.

See itPut the axis at s = 0.25 m, then at 0.50 m. Watch for: the orange bar at 0.125, then four times as tall at 0.500, over an unchanged teal 0.250.
See itKeep s = 0.25 m and raise the mass to 4.0 kg. Watch for: both bars doubling, teal from 0.250 to 0.500 and orange from 0.125 to 0.250.
05

The shift m s² is the same for every shape

The shift involves only the mass and the distance between the axes. Where the mass sits inside the body has already been counted in Icm. At s = 0.25 m and m = 2.0 kg every shape pays the same 0.125 kg·m²:

ShapeIcmm·s²I
Disc0.2500.1250.375
Hoop0.5000.1250.625
Solid sphere0.2000.1250.325
Rod0.0420.1250.167

All values in kg·m². Switching shape moves only the teal bar. A shape with a small Icm, such as the rod, therefore gains the most in proportion when the axis moves.

See itAt s = 0.25 m, switch to the hoop. Watch for: the orange bar staying at 0.125 while the teal bar rises to 0.500 and I reads 0.625.
06

The centre of mass is the cheapest axis

Since m·s² is never negative, I can only grow when the axis leaves the centre of mass. Every parallel axis costs strictly more than the one through the centre of mass. Moving to the rim gives familiar results, with R = 0.50 m and m = 2.0 kg:

  • Disc about its rim: (1/2 + 1) mR² = (3/2) mR² = 0.750 kg·m².
  • Hoop about its rim: 2 mR² = 1.000 kg·m².
  • Solid sphere about a tangent: (7/5) mR² = 0.700 kg·m².
  • Rod about one end, s = 0.25 m: (1/3) mL² = 0.167 kg·m².

The theorem links an axis through the centre of mass to a parallel one. To relate two axes that both miss the centre of mass, go through the centre of mass in between.

See itDrag the axis out to the disc's rim, s = 0.50 m. Watch for: I reading 0.750, three times the teal 0.250.
07

Where it matters

  • Rolling. A rolling disc turns instantaneously about its contact point, a distance R from the centre. I = (1/2)mR² + mR² = (3/2)mR².
  • Swinging bodies. A body hung from a pivot at distance s from its centre of mass is a physical pendulum. Its I about the pivot is Icm + m s².
  • Doors and gates. A uniform door of width L turns about its hinge edge with I = (1/3)mL², from the rod result above.
  • Tabulated values. Handbooks list Icm for standard shapes. The theorem gives the value about any parallel axis from that one number.
08

Summary

In one line. The moment of inertia about an axis parallel to one through the centre of mass is the centre-of-mass value plus an extra term that depends on how far apart the axes are.

Key points

  • I = Icm + m s², for parallel axes only.
  • The shift is the same for every shape. Shape enters only through Icm = c m R².
  • Doubling s quadruples the shift. Doubling m doubles every term.

Common mix-ups

  • "A hoop has a bigger shift than a disc, because it has more inertia." It has a bigger Icm. The shift m·s² is the same for both.
  • "The theorem links any two parallel axes." One of the two axes must pass through the centre of mass.
  • "The centre of mass is the hardest axis to spin about." It is the easiest, because the shift can never be negative.

Things to try on your own

  • Find s for a 2.0 kg hoop at which the shift equals Icm, then check it on the bars.
  • Predict I for the solid sphere at s = 0.40 m and m = 3.0 kg, then set it.
  • At what s does the shift of a 5.0 kg body reach 1.0 kg·m²?
